query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The creation of dual nanoprecipitates during aging (Ni/Ti-enriched L12 and Al/Ti-enriched L21) locally depletes Cr in the matrix and at precipitate–matrix interfaces, which delays the formation of a uniform, protective Cr2O3 scale during oxidation. This delayed Cr-oxide formation exposes fast‐diffusion paths (short-circuit channels) that increase oxidation mass gain at elevated temperatures relative to the uniform as-printed state.
generation.material_initial_state: Selective-laser-melted Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with a >97%-dense, single-fcc cellular microstructure and a uniform Cr distribution (without nanoprecipitates).
generation.intervention: Aging the as-printed material at 750°C for 50 h to generate approximately 25–30 vol% dual nanoprecipitates (Ni/Ti-enriched L12 and larger Al/Ti-enriched, Cr/Fe-depleted L21), predominantly localized near cell walls.
generation.conditions: Isothermal oxidation in oxidizing (or reducing) atmospheres at temperatures ranging from 600°C to 1200°C, with exposure times up to 96 h. Measurements include intermittent mass gain, oxide thickness via cross-sectional microscopy, and detailed phase/element mapping.
generation.structural_mediator: Dual nanoprecipitates that induce localized Cr depletion at the matrix–precipitate interfaces, thus impeding the early, continuous formation of a Cr-rich oxide scale and supplying defect channels (short-circuit paths) for oxygen diffusion.
generation.mechanism: In the as-printed alloy, the uniform Cr distribution facilitates rapid diffusion of Cr outward to form a continuous, protective Cr2O3 barrier that restricts further oxidation. In contrast, in the aged alloy the Cr-depleted regions at nanoprecipitate interfaces hinder uniform Cr2O3 formation, allowing more oxygen to penetrate and react with Al and Ti, forming a mixed duplex-to-trilayer oxide scale with an inner Al/Ti-rich layer. This leads to a higher overall oxidation mass gain, especially at higher temperatures where oxygen diffusion is more rapid.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-printed baseline, the precipitation-aged material will show higher oxidation mass gain, particularly at temperatures above ~900°C, due to delayed and non-uniform protective Cr-scale formation. Both states are expected to exhibit similar activation energies for oxide growth, but the aged state will develop a thicker and less protective inner Al/Ti-rich oxide layer.
generation.baseline: The as-printed alloy with its uniform single-fcc matrix and even Cr distribution, which facilitates early rapid formation of a protective Cr2O3 barrier limiting oxidation.
generation.boundary: The protective effect of the Cr2O3 scale in the as-printed state is effective primarily below ~900°C. The increased oxidation due to precipitate-induced Cr depletion is expected to be pronounced at temperatures above 900°C and observed within the 96-h exposure limit under the test conditions applied.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative impact of the nanoprecipitates on Cr diffusion and the detailed morphology of the oxide scale may vary. Additional microstructural quantification is needed to fully delineate the extent of oxygen diffusion via precipitate–matrix interfaces.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform time-resolved oxidation experiments comparing as-printed and precipitation-aged samples. Use intermittent mass gain measurements, cross-sectional SEM with EDS mapping, XRD, and Raman spectroscopy to compare oxide scale thickness, composition, and morphology across the temperature range (600–1200°C) and over exposure times up to 96 h.
measurements: Mass gain kinetics with power-law fits to extract oxidation rates and activation energies
Cross-sectional oxide scale thickness measurements via SEM
Elemental distribution mapping (especially Cr) via SEM-EDS
Phase identification of oxide constituents via XRD and Raman spectroscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the precipitation-aged alloy does not exhibit a higher oxidation mass gain, delayed formation of a continuous Cr2O3 scale, or significant differences in oxide morphology (e.g., evidence of short-circuit oxygen diffusion paths) compared to the as-printed alloy—particularly at temperatures above 900°C—the hypothesis is falsified.
